item.passage: Transcript: Trelundy infirmary and its weighing scheme. The dispenser's ledger first: it is a costing book. Extra diet, coals, the man's own hours, priced week by week; the total ran heavy enough that the governors twice set the scheme down for debate, and twice let it stand. Occupancy you get elsewhere: bed numbers come from the matron's returns. There are marginal notes, granted, haggling over the price of oatmeal. We date the break from the governors' minutes; the ledger runs unbroken through those years. The weighing itself. Physicians read the charts as a record of recovery. The ward staff had quite other ends in view: Friday's figures settled who could be put to work on the ward. The scale came in with a physician in the house's first month, and the kitchen inspections start twenty years later. Someone asked whether the balance was swapped — it was the same beam throughout. And the weighing did fix the shape of the week; true, though it is not my point. Maderwyn re-read the registers. Weight and length of stay track each other far more loosely than the reports of the day claimed. Winter and summer intakes gained at much the same rate. The gains scatter across quarter-ounces. The attendants' books disagree constantly rather than running alike. Rostrellick says the weighing shaped admission. His notes come from the eighteen sixties, a generation after the weighing began.
